title: Sima Qian Completes His Father's History
text:
Sima Tan was Grand Astrologer at the court of the Han emperor Wu, an office that also kept records. He had begun to compile a history of China from the earliest times. In 110 BC, when the emperor performed the great sacrifice at Mount Tai, Sima Tan fell ill and was left behind at Luoyang. His son Sima Qian found him dying there.

Sima Qian recorded the scene in the last chapter of his history. His father took his hand, wept, and charged him to become Grand Astrologer in his turn and to complete the history, so that the deeds of rulers and worthy men would not be forgotten. Sima Qian bowed and promised.

He took up his father's office. Then, in 99 BC, he spoke up at court in defense of a general, Li Ling, who had surrendered to the Xiongnu. The emperor was enraged, and Sima Qian was sentenced to death. He could have chosen death with honor. Instead he accepted castration, the most shameful punishment, so that he could live to finish the work.

In a letter to his friend Ren An, he explained that every man must die, but that some deaths weigh more than Mount Tai and others less than a feather. He could not die with his work unfinished. The result, the Records of the Grand Historian, became the model for Chinese history writing for two thousand years.
lesson: A promise to a parent can give strength to endure what seems unbearable. Some work is worth finishing because of whom we are finishing it for.
people: Sima Qian, Sima Tan, Emperor Wu of Han
source: Sima Qian, Shiji (Records of the Grand Historian), chapter 130; Letter to Ren An (Han Shu 62)
